hints.title: Rearrangement and Sorting Obstacle
hints.text: Sorting both strings takes superlinear time and rearranging characters directly is expensive. If two strings are anagrams, what must be identical about their constituent characters?

hints.title: Character Frequency Invariant
hints.text: Two strings are anagrams if and only if they have identical lengths and every distinct character appears the exact same number of times in both.

hints.title: Single Frequency Table Balance
hints.text: First check if the lengths of both strings match. Then count occurrences of each character in the first string and decrement counts for the second string. If every character count resolves to zero, the strings are anagrams.

hints.title: Complete Implementation

variables: N: length of strings s and t (1 <= N <= 5 * 10^4)
complexity.notes: Single pass counting with fixed alphabet size K = 26 gives O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity.whyNaiveFails: Sorting both strings costs O(N log N) time. For large inputs, this adds unnecessary overhead compared to single-pass frequency counting, and generating permutations takes factorial O(N!) time.
complexity.spaceTimeTradeoff: Using O(K) frequency table space where K <= 26 allows O(N) time with minimal constant space overhead, strictly better than O(N log N) sorting.
complexity.interviewerExpectation: Length equality check first, single array or map for frequency counting, awareness of Unicode vs ASCII character sets, and O(1) space justification when alphabet is fixed.

solutions.approach: One-Pass Frequency Counting with Early Exit
